title: Fuel for the work required
goal: Plan a week that matches carbohydrate to each session, explain the glycogen threshold idea, weigh it against simply eating high-carbohydrate, and name its risks.

steps.title: Match the fuel to the session
steps.text:
Train-low research left a practical model: [carbohydrate periodisation](g:carbohydrate-periodisation), or 'fuel for the work required'. Instead of restricting carbohydrate for weeks, you adjust it **day by day and meal by meal** to the intensity, duration and goal of the next session [[c:per-model]].

The rule of thumb: keep hard sessions fuelled. Train-low is best kept to sessions that don't depend on carbohydrate, such as steady riding or running below the [lactate threshold](g:lactate-threshold) [[c:per-easy-only]]. Intervals, races and race-pace work get full stores and carbohydrate during.

How many grams a day each kind of day needs is in *Carbohydrate, fat and protein metabolism*.

claims.text: In the 'fuel for the work required' model, carbohydrate availability is adjusted day to day and meal by meal to the intensity, duration and goals of training, rather than restricted chronically.

evidence.quote: As opposed to chronic periods of CHO restriction, this model suggests that CHO availability should be manipulated day-to-day and meal-by-meal according to the intensity, duration and specific training goals.

claims.text: Train-low may be best kept to sessions that are not carbohydrate-dependent, such as steady sessions below the lactate threshold.

evidence.quote: Intuitively, ‘train low’ may be best left to those training sessions that are not CHO-dependent and where the intensity and duration is not likely to be compromised by reduced CHO availability (e.g. steady-state-type training sessions performed at intensities below the lactate threshold).

steps.title: The glycogen threshold idea
steps.text:
How low is low enough? Looking across train-low studies, Impey and colleagues saw the extra adaptations mainly when sessions began with muscle glycogen at or below about **300 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry muscle** [[c:per-300]]. (The trained cyclists in the train-low lesson had 478 when fed normally.) Go under about **100**, and signals for building muscle protein may be turned down.

That gives the [glycogen threshold](g:glycogen-threshold) hypothesis: a window of roughly **100–300 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry** that is low enough to amplify the signal but high enough to still do the planned work [[c:per-window]].

It is a hypothesis: athletes can't measure their own glycogen before a ride, and the glycogen cost of real sessions is still being worked out.

claims.text: Adaptations to carbohydrate restriction are particularly evident when pre-exercise muscle glycogen is at or below about 300 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry.

evidence.quote: In this regard, examination of available train-low studies (see Table 1 ) demonstrates that adaptations associated with CHO restriction are particularly evident when absolute pre-exercise muscle glycogen concentrations are ≤ 300 mmol/kg dw.

claims.text: The glycogen threshold hypothesis proposes a window (about 100–300 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry) that permits the required training and activates adaptive signalling; below about 100 may reduce protein-synthesis signalling. The glycogen cost of habitual sessions still has to be quantified.

evidence.quote: Herein, we present our rationale for the glycogen threshold hypothesis, a window of muscle glycogen concentrations that simultaneously permits completion of required training workloads and activation of the molecular machinery regulating training adaptations.
300–100 mmol/kg dw) that is permissive to facilitating the required training intensity, acute cell signalling responses and post-exercise remodelling processes
< 100 mmol/kg dw) may reduce the regulation of protein synthesis pathways
In order to strategically implement train-low sessions, our challenge now is to quantify the glycogen cost of habitual training sessions

steps.title: A periodised week in practice
steps.text:
Impey's example: eat plenty of carbohydrate before, during and after a hard session on day 1, then cut it at the evening meal. Sleep low, and do day 2's easier session with little or no carbohydrate beforehand [[c:per-example]]. Then refuel for the next hard day.

| day | session | carbohydrate |
|---|---|---|
| Tue | intervals (evening) | high before, during, after; low dinner |
| Wed | easy 90 min (morning) | fasted ride, refuel after |
| Thu | rest or easy | moderate |
| Sat | long ride, race-pace blocks | high, plus carbohydrate during |

The daily total can stay the same. In the sleep-low trial both groups ate 6 g·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹; only the timing moved [[c:per-same-total]].

claims.text: A practical example: high carbohydrate before, during and after a hard session on day 1, reduced at the evening meal, then sleep-low and train-low for a lower-intensity session on day 2.

evidence.quote: In this example, high CHO intake is advised before, during and after the training session on day 1 (e.g. ‘train high’), but reduced in the evening meal to facilitate sleep low and train low for a lower-intensity session on day 2

claims.text: In the sleep-low trial both groups ate the same daily carbohydrate (6 g·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹), with different timing around sessions.

evidence.quote: consumed the same daily carbohydrate (CHO) intake (6 g·kg(-1)·d(-1)) but with different timing over the day to manipulate CHO availability before and after training sessions

steps.title: How much carbohydrate moves on a sleep-low night?
steps.problem: A 70 kg triathlete eats 6 g·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹ of carbohydrate. Her dinner normally holds a quarter of it. On a sleep-low night, that dinner carbohydrate is moved to after the next morning's easy ride. How many grams move?
steps: So about 105 g moves from dinner to the recovery breakfast and lunch; the day's total is unchanged.

steps.title: Periodised or simply high-carb?
steps.text:
Is periodising better than just eating plenty all the time? In the first Supernova study, the periodised group improved its 10 km race walk by 5.3% and the always-high group by 6.6%: both clearly beat LCHF, neither clearly beat the other [[c:per-supernova]]. The meta-analysis in the train-low lesson found no overall gain in well-trained athletes [[c:per-meta]].

Supporters reply that the trials are short (1–4 weeks), and that elite athletes train 20–30 h a week while most studies used under 10 h [[c:per-short]].

Fair summary: periodising is a reasonable way to eat, not a proven performance boost.

claims.text: Diets with chronic or periodised high carbohydrate availability both supported performance gains in elite race walkers, unlike LCHF.

evidence.quote: In contrast to training with diets providing chronic or periodised high carbohydrate availability, adaptation to an LCHF diet impairs performance in elite endurance athletes despite a significant improvement in peak aerobic capacity.
HCHO and PCHO groups improved times for 10 km race walk: 6.6% (90% CI: 4.1, 9.1%) and 5.3% (3.4, 7.2%), with no improvement (-1.6% (-8.5, 5.3%)) for the LCHF group.

claims.text: Periodised carbohydrate restriction does not per se enhance performance in endurance-trained athletes.

evidence.quote: Based on the available literature, we therefore conclude that periodized CHO restriction does not per se enhance performance in endurance-trained athletes.

claims.text: Included trials lasted 1–4 weeks; elite athletes may train 20–30 h a week, whereas most studies used under 10 h a week.

evidence.quote: The durations of the included training studies varied from one to 4 weeks and the number of participants from 11 to 26
Additionally, elite athletes may also undertake 20–30 h of training per week, whereas many of the study designs reviewed thus far have utilized training programmes of < 10 h per week.

debate.question: Does periodising carbohydrate improve endurance performance more than a consistently high-carbohydrate diet?

sides.position: Yes, potentially: low glycogen amplifies training signals, and sleep-low trials improved efficiency and 10 km run times in triathletes.
Not shown: in well-trained athletes, randomised trials and a meta-analysis find no extra performance gain over high carbohydrate.

steps.title: The risks: energy, illness, bone
steps.text:
Cutting carbohydrate often cuts energy too. Endurance athletes already face daily spells of carbohydrate and calorie restriction from multiple sessions a day, and longer spells of low [energy availability](g:energy-availability) [[c:per-lea]]. Repeated daily training with low carbohydrate may also make illness more likely [[c:per-illness]].

Bone: in world-class race walkers, 3.5 weeks of a ketogenic diet impaired [bone turnover markers](g:bone-turnover-markers) (less building, more breakdown); a return to carbohydrate restored only the breakdown marker [[c:per-bone]]. These are blood markers, not fractures.

The 2023 IOC consensus on [REDs](g:reds) names low carbohydrate availability as a growing part of the picture [[c:per-ioc]]. More in *Energy availability and RED-S*.

claims.text: Many endurance athletes have daily periods of combined carbohydrate and calorie restriction from multiple sessions a day, and longer periods of suboptimal energy availability.

evidence.quote: many endurance athletes present daily with transient periods of both CHO and calorie restriction due to multiple training sessions per day, as well as longer-term periods of suboptimal energy availability

claims.text: Repeated daily training with reduced carbohydrate availability may increase susceptibility to illness.

evidence.quote: Additionally, repetitive daily training in the face of a reduction in CHO availability (so as to reduce pre-exercise muscle glycogen concentration) may increase susceptibility to illness

claims.text: A 3.5-week ketogenic LCHF diet impaired markers of bone modelling/remodelling in elite race walkers; acute carbohydrate restoration recovered only the resorption marker.

evidence.quote: Markers of bone modeling/remodeling were impaired after short-term LCHF diet, and only a marker of resorption recovered after acute CHO restoration.

claims.text: The 2023 IOC REDs consensus reports emerging data on the growing role of low carbohydrate availability.

evidence.quote: emerging data demonstrating the growing role of low carbohydrate availability

points: 'Fuel for the work required': adjust carbohydrate day by day and meal by meal to each session; keep hard sessions fuelled and do train-low only on easy, steady ones.
The glycogen threshold hypothesis proposes a window of about 100–300 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry: low enough to boost the signal, high enough to do the work.
A typical pattern: high carbohydrate around a hard session, low dinner, fasted easy session next morning, then refuel; the daily total can stay the same.
Compared with simply eating high-carbohydrate, periodising has not been shown to improve performance in trained athletes.
Risks: low energy availability, illness and worse bone markers; see Energy availability and RED-S.

variants.stem: Which session in a cyclist's week is the best candidate for low carbohydrate availability?

options.text: A 90 min easy endurance ride below the lactate threshold
options.why: Right: steady, low-intensity work isn't carbohydrate-dependent, so quality doesn't suffer.

options.text: 5 × 5 min intervals near VO₂max
options.why: Hard intervals depend on carbohydrate; low availability would cost intensity.

options.text: A 40 km time-trial rehearsal at race pace
options.why: Race-pace work should be fuelled like the race.

options.text: A sprint session with 10 all-out efforts
options.why: Sprints run on PCr and glycogen; this needs full stores.

variants.stem: Which session in a runner's week is the best candidate for low carbohydrate availability?

options.text: An easy 60 min run at conversational pace
options.why: Right: steady, low-intensity work isn't carbohydrate-dependent, so quality doesn't suffer.

options.text: A 30 min tempo run at threshold pace
options.why: Threshold work depends heavily on carbohydrate; low availability would cost pace.

options.text: 10 × 400 m repeats
options.why: Hard intervals need full stores to hit their target pace.

options.text: A half-marathon race
options.why: Races are 'compete high': fully fuelled.

variants.stem: A triathlete says: 'I periodise my carbs: low Monday to Friday, high at weekends.' Her Tuesday and Thursday hold her hardest bike intervals. What is wrong with her plan, judged by 'fuel for the work required'?

options.text: Her hard weekday sessions go unfuelled
options.why: Right: carbohydrate should follow each session's demand, not the calendar; hard sessions get high availability.

options.text: Nothing: any weekly rotation counts
options.why: Rotation alone isn't the model; it matches fuel to the work.

options.text: Her weekends should be low too
options.why: That would make it chronic restriction, close to keto, which impaired performance.

options.text: It only works for runners
options.why: The sleep-low trial with gains was in triathletes; sport isn't the issue.

variants.stem: Before an easy ride, a cyclist's muscle glycogen is estimated at 150 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry. Under the glycogen threshold hypothesis, where does this sit?

options.text: Inside the window: low enough to amplify the signal, high enough to train
options.why: Right: 150 lies within about 100–300.

options.text: Above the window: too high to add extra signal
options.why: Above the window means over about 300.

options.text: Below the window: protein-building signals may be turned down
options.why: That applies under about 100.

options.text: So low that no exercise is possible
options.why: Exercise is possible at much lower levels; the window is about adaptation, not ability to move.

variants.stem: Before an easy run, a runner's muscle glycogen is estimated at 60 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry. Under the glycogen threshold hypothesis, where does this sit?

options.text: Below the window: protein-building signals may be turned down
options.why: Right: under about 100 may reduce protein-synthesis signalling.

options.text: Inside the window: the ideal train-low level
options.why: The window is about 100–300; 60 is under it.

options.text: Above the window: too high to add extra signal
options.why: Above the window means over about 300.

options.text: Normal for a fed, rested athlete
options.why: Fed, rested trained muscle holds several hundred (478 in the train-low study).

variants.stem: Before a morning swim, a triathlete's muscle glycogen is estimated at 450 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry. Under the glycogen threshold hypothesis, where does this sit?

options.text: Above the window: little extra signal from low glycogen
options.why: Right: 450 is above about 300, near the normal fed level.

options.text: Inside the window: the ideal train-low level
options.why: The window is about 100–300; 450 is above it.

options.text: Below the window: protein-building signals may be turned down
options.why: That applies under about 100.

options.text: Dangerously low: the session should be cancelled
options.why: 450 is a normal, well-fed level.

variants.stem: Why is the glycogen threshold still a hypothesis rather than a training rule?

options.text: It rests on indirect evidence that can't yet be applied
options.why: Right: it comes from comparing studies, athletes can't measure their own glycogen, and the glycogen cost of real sessions still needs measuring.

options.text: A large randomised trial disproved it
options.why: No such trial exists; it hasn't been tested directly.

options.text: It applies only to female athletes
options.why: Nothing in it is sex-specific; most data are from men.

options.text: Glycogen has no link to training signals
options.why: Low glycogen did amplify signals in most studies; the exact threshold is the open question.

variants.stem: A runner weighing 64 kg eats 6 g·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹ of carbohydrate. On a sleep-low night, dinner, normally a third of the day's carbohydrate, is moved to after the next morning's ride. How many grams move?

options.text: About 128 g
options.why: Right: 64 × 6 = 384 g a day; a third of it is 128 g.

options.text: About 384 g
options.why: This is the whole day's carbohydrate: the fraction for dinner was left out.

options.text: About 2.00 g
options.why: This takes the fraction of the g·kg⁻¹ figure and forgets to multiply by body mass.

options.text: About 192 g
options.why: This uses a half instead of a third.

variants.solution: Daily total = 64 kg × 6 g·kg⁻¹ = 384 g. Dinner share = 384 × 0.333 = 128 g moved to the next morning.

variants.stem: A cyclist weighing 80 kg eats 6 g·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹ of carbohydrate. On a sleep-low night, dinner, normally a quarter of the day's carbohydrate, is moved to after the next morning's ride. How many grams move?

options.text: About 120 g
options.why: Right: 80 × 6 = 480 g a day; a quarter of it is 120 g.

options.text: About 480 g
options.why: This is the whole day's carbohydrate: the fraction for dinner was left out.

options.text: About 1.50 g
options.why: This takes the fraction of the g·kg⁻¹ figure and forgets to multiply by body mass.

options.text: About 160 g
options.why: This uses a third instead of a quarter.

variants.solution: Daily total = 80 kg × 6 g·kg⁻¹ = 480 g. Dinner share = 480 × 0.25 = 120 g moved to the next morning.

variants.stem: A triathlete weighing 55 kg eats 7 g·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹ of carbohydrate. On a sleep-low night, dinner, normally a quarter of the day's carbohydrate, is moved to after the next morning's ride. How many grams move?

options.text: About 96 g
options.why: Right: 55 × 7 = 385 g a day; a quarter of it is 96 g.

options.text: About 385 g
options.why: This is the whole day's carbohydrate: the fraction for dinner was left out.

options.text: About 1.75 g
options.why: This takes the fraction of the g·kg⁻¹ figure and forgets to multiply by body mass.

options.text: About 128 g
options.why: This uses a third instead of a quarter.

variants.solution: Daily total = 55 kg × 7 g·kg⁻¹ = 385 g. Dinner share = 385 × 0.25 = 96 g moved to the next morning.

variants.stem: A cyclist has VO₂max intervals on Thursday evening and an easy endurance ride on Friday morning. How does a sleep-low plan arrange carbohydrate?

options.text: High for Thursday's intervals, low dinner, Friday's ride fasted
options.why: Right: train high for the hard session, then sleep low and train low for the easy one.

options.text: Low before Thursday's intervals, high before Friday's ride
options.why: Backwards: the hard session gets the fuel, the easy one goes low.

options.text: Thursday's intervals fasted, Friday's ride after a big breakfast
options.why: Fasted VO₂max intervals would lose intensity; the easy ride is the one to do low.

options.text: Low carbohydrate on both days to double the signal
options.why: Two low days in a row would cost the hard session and add to low energy availability.

variants.stem: A coach asks: 'Should my well-trained riders switch from always-high carbohydrate to periodised carbohydrate to get faster?' What is the best evidence-based answer?

options.text: No extra speed is proven, but it's a reasonable way to eat
options.why: Right: trials and a meta-analysis show no clear gain over high carbohydrate, and no harm when done this way.

options.text: Yes: it reliably makes athletes about 3% faster
options.why: Only Marquet's two unblinded trials found gains like that.

options.text: No: periodising harms performance just as keto does
options.why: In Supernova the periodised group improved 5.3%, much like the high group; it's keto that harmed.

options.text: Yes, but only if they eat keto between hard sessions
options.why: Chronic keto blunted performance; periodising keeps carbohydrate in the diet.

variants.stem: Supporters of periodisation say the trials don't settle the question. Which limitation is fair?

options.text: Trials were short and low-volume
options.why: Right: trials lasted 1–4 weeks, mostly under 10 h a week, while elites train 20–30 h a week for years; effects that build over a career could be missed.

options.text: Trials had too many athletes
options.why: They had only 11–26 participants each.

options.text: Blinding hid the effect
options.why: Most weren't blinded; and blinding removes bias, it doesn't hide real effects.

options.text: Trials only measured fat use
options.why: The meta-analysis included only studies that measured endurance performance.

variants.stem: A runner does sleep-low four nights a week, has lost 3 kg in a month without meaning to, and keeps catching colds. What is the most likely problem?

options.text: Carbohydrate restriction has become low energy availability, a REDs risk
options.why: Right: unplanned weight loss and frequent illness suggest too little energy, not just strategic low-carbohydrate sessions.

options.text: Train-low is working: weight loss shows good adaptation
options.why: Unplanned weight loss with frequent illness is a warning sign, not a training effect.

options.text: Too much carbohydrate on her hard days
options.why: Excess carbohydrate wouldn't cause weight loss and colds.

options.text: Ordinary bad luck with viruses
options.why: Possible, but the pattern of restriction, weight loss and illness points to low energy availability.

variants.stem: In the elite race walkers who ate a ketogenic diet for 3.5 weeks, what did the bone turnover markers show?

options.text: Less building, more breakdown; refuelling fixed only breakdown
options.why: Right: formation markers stayed down after carbohydrate came back.

options.text: More bone building, thanks to the weight-bearing walking
options.why: All groups walked; the keto group's building markers fell.

options.text: A doubling of stress fractures in the keto group
options.why: These were blood markers over weeks, not fractures.

options.text: No change from baseline in any marker
options.why: Markers changed clearly in the keto group.
